newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE-Drug problems haunt Bangladeshi homes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Drug problems haunt Bangladeshi homes.

text.p: Nargis Akhtar wept as she remembered the day her drug addict husband died.
The promising young surgeon had become addicted to pethidine, an injectable pain reliever given to patients after operations.

Knowing of his addiction, the family admitted him to a drug rehabilitation clinic in Dhaka for two months. But less than a year after he was discharged, relatives and colleagues found Nurul Islam dead with six empty ampules of pethidine beside him.
"My husband looked completely recovered. I was so happy. He joined his hospital job. But he relapsed in just six months," said Akhtar, a mother of two and now a 34-year-old widow.
UNEMPLOYMENT ADDS TO DRUGS MENACE
With Asian and religious values under pressure, drugs haunt families across Bangladesh, an impoverished South Asian country of 120 million people with a per capita income of just $240.
Growing unemployment adds to the problem.
"Bangladesh is no longer a transit country, it itself is becoming a market for drugs," said Khondker A. Hafiz, coordinator of the United Nations Drug Control Programme (UNDCP) in Bangladesh.
"You can't name a single squatter area in Dhaka where you won't find heroin. Harder drugs are increasingly available on streets," he said.
What was particularly alarming was that drugs were penetrating rural, low income areas, he said.
Bangladesh has no official estimate of how many addicts there are in the country, but the UNDCP estimates the number could be between one and two million.
The largest circulated Bangla-language newspaper, Ittefaq, reported last month there were at least 700,000 drug addicts in 16 northern districts alone.
Some 400 young men died of drug addiction and 1,500 became disabled during the last three years in the northern region, the newspaper said, quoting a survey by a voluntary health organisation.
Doctors at Dhaka's drug rehabilitation clinics said the number of people seeking treatment was rising every day.
Police are increasingly linking crime in the country to drugs. A UNDCP survey said 46 percent of drug users were involved in some kind of criminal activity.
AUTHORITIES SLOW TO RESPOND
The government, however, is still reluctant to admit there is a major problem.
"It's true cases are increasing. But compared to the global situation, Bangladesh is not alarming," said Nazmul Ahsan Chowdhury, director general of the Department of Narcotics Control DNC).
He thinks Bangladesh is more a transit country than a market for harder drugs like heroin.
"Bangladesh's location and huge land frontier (with India and Burma) has made it an ideal corridor," said Chowdhury.
The country is sandwiched between two major poppy growing regions -- the Golden Triangle of Burma, Thailand and Laos, and the Golden Crescent comprising Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran.
Narcotics control agencies said an Indian-manufactured cough syrup made of codeine phosphate was the most widely used drug in Bangladesh.
"It may sound peculiar, but Phensidyl (the brand name of the Indian-manufactured cough syrup) is our single biggest concern," Chowdhury said.
Bangladesh banned production of cough syrup with codeine phosphate, a substance derived from opium, in 1982. COTTAGE INDUSTRY DRUGS
"We have heard cottage industry-like plants have mushroomed on the Indian side of the border to manufacture codeine phosphate syrup for the Bangladesh market", said one UNDCP official.
Doctors at a Dhaka hospital said they were receiving increasing numbers of patients with severe kidney damage and linked it to prolonged use of codeine.
Also flowing in from India are synthetic pain-relieving, injectible drugs like Tidijesic -- used as a veterinary analgesic -- and dozens of sleeping pill brands.
The DNC wants an agreement with the Indian government on joint monitoring of drugs on borders.
But with politicians appearing relaxed on the issue, officials complain there have been lapses in enforcing anti-drugs laws.
Bangladesh's 1990 Drug Control Act provides the death penalty for possessing 25 grams or more of heroin. No one has ever been hanged.
Few people are even arrested for possession and the penalties handed down tend to be jail terms of only a few years or fines.
With a small budget and poor logistics, the DNC says it lacks the teeth to crush organised drug networks.
"We have only 500 enforcers countrywide, poorly equipped," the DNC chief said.
The agency is trying to reduce demand by involving communities in an awareness campaign and introducing drug education to schools.

Teachers, judges, religious leaders, lawyers and police are regularly invited to workshops and some 60 voluntary organisations have been given financial help to campaign against drugs at the grassroot level.
But the programmes are mostly funded by UNDCP and some think it should be getting more help.
"I think there should be a much stronger political commitment to fight drugs," Chowdhury said.
